I am 47 years old and have farmed these lands in Quzhou for 25 years. With 232.9 mu and only three people in my household, I cannot afford to take big risks or spread myself too thin. The wheat–maize rotation is my backbone—it is stable, the buyers are reliable, and I know exactly how to manage it. I will put 200 mu into that double-cropping system. Cauliflower brings better prices, but it is heavy on labor and transplanting, so I will keep it to 32.9 mu this year, planted in spring and harvested before the maize goes in. I have a well, so I can irrigate when the rains fail, but I do not waste water. For wheat I rotary-till the land and apply a basal compound fertilizer plus one topdressing of urea; for maize I use no-tillage after wheat harvest to save time and fuel, which is what most neighbors here do. I use improved wheat varieties and hybrid maize seed because they outperform traditional seed every year. For cauliflower I buy improved seedlings from the market, rotary-till the plot well, and give it more fertilizer and more pesticide sprays since vegetable buyers are picky about quality. My target yields are what I usually achieve: about 500 kg/mu for wheat, 550 kg/mu for maize, and around 3,000 kg/mu for cauliflower.
